title: You Picture Pavlov Ringing a Dinner Bell, Yet One Metronome Rewired Digestion
description:
Clinical Case Briefing — Ivan Pavlov's dogs and classical conditioning (St. Petersburg, Institute of Experimental Medicine, 1890s-1900s), grounded in Pavlov, I. P. (1903) (Lecture II read in full (Classics in the History of Psychology, York University)). Empirical findings show that pavlov received the 1904 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine 'in recognition of his work on the physiology of digestion', not for conditioned reflexes.

At the circuit level, this episode examines how auditory cortex, brainstem coordinate behavioral and neural responses, alongside evidence that to measure saliva, each dog first had a minor operation that moved the opening of a salivary duct from inside the mouth to the outside of the cheek (parotid) or under the chin (submaxillary), so saliva flowed out onto the skin.

Primary Peer-Reviewed Sources:
- Pavlov, I. P. (1927). Conditioned Reflexes: An Investigation of the Physiological Activity of the Cerebral Cortex (G. V. Anrep, Trans. & Ed.). London: Oxford University Press. Lecture II read in full (Classics in the History of Psychology, York University).
- Pavlov, I. P. (2010). Conditioned reflexes: An investigation of the physiological activity of the cerebral cortex. Annals of Neurosciences, 17(3), 136-141 (reprint of the 1927 Anrep translation excerpt). https://doi.org/10.5214/ans.0972-7531.1017309
- Pavlov, I. P. (1906). The scientific investigation of the psychical faculties or processes in the higher animals. Science, 24(620), 613-619. https://doi.org/10.1126/science.24.620.613

AI Disclosure: Visual reenactments, 3D anatomical models, and narration in this documentary Short were produced with AI synthesis tools from verified peer-reviewed sources.
